slides.title: Lecture 2: Supervised
slides.summary: Lecture 2 introduces supervised learning and the k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) algorithm within the context of machine learning and inductive inference. The session is presented by Sieben Bocklandt, utilizing slide decks originally developed by Jesse Davis for the Principles of Machine Learning course.

slides.title: - Understand the basic goal of inductive supervised learning
slides.summary: This slide outlines the primary learning objectives for the lecture, starting with understanding the basic goal of inductive supervised learning. It further lists essential topics including feature construction, the definition of a hypothesis, and the components of a learning algorithm. The goals also cover the importance of the kNN algorithm, its mechanics regarding distance measures and decision surfaces, and strategies to address its associated pitfalls.

slides.title: Traditional programming
slides.summary: The lecture contrasts traditional programming with supervised machine learning by illustrating their distinct input-output flows. In traditional programming, a computer combines data and a program to produce an output. Conversely, in supervised learning, the computer uses data and the desired output to generate the program itself.

slides.title: - Given a set of data consisting of < x , y > with
slides.summary: Supervised learning operates on a dataset composed of pairs denoted as <x, y>. In this framework, x represents a set of features, while y is the label associated with those specific features. This pairing of inputs and their corresponding outputs forms the fundamental data structure for supervised learning tasks.

slides.title: - Given a set of data consisting of < x , y > with
slides.summary: Supervised learning involves training a model using a dataset of input features ($x$) and their corresponding labels ($y$). Unlike traditional programming, which combines data with a fixed program to produce output, machine learning uses paired inputs and outputs to learn the underlying program or hypothesis. The goal is to derive a function that can accurately map new feature sets ($x'$) to predicted outputs ($y'$).

slides.title: - Evaluating, filtering, manipulating and encoding data to make sure the ML model
slides.summary: Data preprocessing involves evaluating, filtering, manipulating, and encoding data to ensure machine learning models can effectively utilize it. Key techniques include handling missing values (e.g., removing examples or adding mean values), scaling variables to uniform forms, removing outliers like random noise, and converting non-numerical data into numerical formats. Additionally, the most critical step is dividing the dataset into three distinct sets: training for model development, validation for tuning, and testing for final evaluation.

slides.title: - Which features can describe a song?
slides.summary: Feature construction involves defining attributes that describe a song, such as genre, duration, tempo (BPM), key, loudness (dB), acousticness, energy, and whether it is instrumental. These features are categorized into objective values, like duration and tempo, and subjective values, including acousticness and energy. Defining these features is essential because they characterize the problem and form the basis for building and evaluating models.

slides.title: - Features describe the problem
slides.summary: Features describe the problem and are known by various names depending on the domain: attributes in databases, covariates in statistical learning, variables in probabilistic learning, and KPIs in business applications. Defining features is a critical skill rather than a mechanical process because there is no ground truth; poor feature selection directly results in poor model performance. Additionally, features can take different forms, such as boolean values represented as true/false or 1/0 in code.

slides.title: - Boolean (1/0 ; True/False)
slides.summary: The lecture outlines five feature types: Boolean (e.g., Instrumental={True, False}), Nominal with no value relationship (e.g., Genre), Linear/Ordered with structured values (e.g., Energy={Low, Medium, High}), Numerical integers (e.g., BPM), and Hierarchical features with partial IS-A ordering. The professor clarifies that nominal categories like music genres lack inherent order, whereas ordered features like energy levels possess a defined structure from low to high.

slides.title: Features: properties that describe the problem
slides.summary: Features are properties that describe a problem for any given data point, such as a song or image. These features form a fixed-length vector, ensuring every data point shares the same structure with a consistent number of attributes like genre or beat. While missing data may occur and require specific handling strategies, this fixed structure allows models to reliably process new inputs using a defined set of features.

slides.title: Features: properties that describe the problem
slides.summary: Features are properties that describe a problem by converting a new data point, such as a song or image, into a fixed-length feature vector. This process involves defining $m$ specific attributes to represent the data; for example, a song can be described using features like title, genre, BPM, key, and whether it is instrumental.

slides.title: Features: properties that describe the problem
slides.summary: Features are properties that describe a problem, used to construct a fixed-length feature vector for any data point like a song. This involves defining specific attributes such as title, genre, BPM, key, and instrumental status, where each feature has a distinct domain type including string, nominal, numerical, or boolean. In supervised learning contexts, these features are paired with a label, such as whether the item belongs to a playlist, to fully characterize the data instance.

slides.title: Features: properties that describe the problem
slides.summary: Features are properties that describe a problem, where each new data point is defined by $m$ features with specific value domains based on their type. Consequently, every example is represented as a fixed-length vector of these $m$ feature values, potentially accompanied by a class label. For instance, a song can be characterized by string titles, nominal genres, numerical BPMs, and boolean attributes like instrumental status.

slides.title: - Assume a fixed form for the relationship between the features and the target
slides.summary: This slide defines an approach where a fixed functional form for the relationship between features and the target is assumed before observing any data. This constraint results in hypothesis classes of a fixed size, limiting the model's flexibility to specific predefined structures rather than adapting freely to the dataset.

slides.title: - Assume a fixed form for the relationship between the features and the target
slides.summary: This slide defines fixed-size hypothesis classes where the relationship between features and targets assumes a specific structural form prior to observing data. Within this framework, the model's structure remains constant while only its parameters vary, such as using straight lines or hyperplanes to divide feature space. Canonical examples of this approach include linear regression, logistic regression, and Naïve Bayes.

slides.title: - Structure and form of the model changes during learning, often becoming more
slides.summary: Variable-size hypothesis classes differ from fixed-structure models because their form changes during learning, often becoming more complex as data increases. Canonical examples include decision trees, which grow by adding new nodes, and rule sets, which expand by incorporating additional rules. Unlike models with a constant mathematical description where only weights vary, these structures dynamically adapt their complexity to the learning process.

slides.title: Learning a model
slides.summary: Learning a model

slides.title: - Given
slides.summary: The overall learning objective for binary classification assumes a given set of positive and negative examples. These examples are drawn independently at random from an unknown probability distribution. This setup establishes the fundamental data conditions required to train a binary classifier.

slides.title: - Given
slides.summary: Given positive and negative examples drawn independently from an unknown probability distribution, the objective is to learn a model that classifies most positives correctly while excluding negatives. Crucially, the model must generalize to correctly label future examples rather than merely memorizing the training set, which would constitute overfitting. This binary classification framework can be extended to scenarios with more than two classes.

slides.title: - Suppose I have a problem with 4 binary features and 2 classes
slides.summary: This slide illustrates the fundamental challenge of learning by analyzing a problem with four binary features and two classes, which creates a feature space of 16 possible examples. Despite this small space, there are 65,536 distinct ways to label these examples, meaning observing only a subset of data leaves many potential models consistent with the training set. Consequently, deciding which model is best remains difficult because partial observation does not sufficiently rule out alternative hypotheses.

slides.title: - We need to make assumptions: experience alone doesn’t allow us to make
slides.summary: Experience alone cannot determine conclusions for unseen data instances, necessitating assumptions known as inductive bias to guide model selection within a vast hypothesis space. Inductive bias consists of two types: restriction, which limits the hypothesis space to specific forms like rules or linear models, and preference, which imposes an ordering on hypotheses, such as favoring simpler models over complex ones.

slides.title: - At high-level, algorithms learn one of these:
slides.summary: At a high level, algorithms learn one of three primary structures: a function that predicts a class or real value, such as decision trees and linear regression; a conditional probability distribution P(Y|X), exemplified by logistic regression and neural networks; or a joint probability distribution P(X,Y), as seen in Naïve Bayes. These categories define the fundamental goals of learning algorithms.

slides.title: - At high-level, algorithms learn one of these:
slides.summary: At a high level, algorithms learn one of three targets: a function predicting class or real values (e.g., decision trees), a conditional probability distribution P(Y|X) (e.g., logistic regression), or a joint probability distribution P(X,Y) (e.g., Naïve Bayes). Learning a model follows a two-step approach involving searching through the hypothesis space and evaluating candidate hypotheses. This process continues by tweaking parameters until a satisfactory model is found, balancing simplicity against performance costs.

slides.title: - Discrete:
slides.summary: Discrete model building involves selecting a specific architecture or configuration from a hypothesis space using combinatorial search methods like best-first, depth-first, or beam-search. This process addresses decisions regarding hyperparameter choices and includes techniques such as decision trees, feature selection, and rule learning to navigate the available options effectively.

slides.title: - Discrete:
slides.summary: Searching the hypothesis space involves two approaches: discrete and continuous. Discrete search determines "what model to build" using combinatorial methods like best-first or beam-search for choices such as architecture, hyperparameters, decision trees, feature selection, and rule learning. In contrast, continuous search addresses "what numbers the model should contain," utilizing optimization techniques like gradient descent to tune weights and parameters in fixed-structure models such as neural networks.

slides.title: - Typically we have two high-level components:
slides.summary: Evaluating candidate models typically involves assessing two high-level components. The first component measures how well the model fits the data, while the second evaluates the complexity of the model itself. These factors are central to determining the overall quality and suitability of a candidate model.

slides.title: - Typically we have two high-level components:
slides.summary: Evaluating candidate models involves balancing two high-level components: how well the model fits the data and its complexity. The goal is to trade off good fit against bad complexity, ideally achieving a perfect fit with minimal complexity. In rule learning, this is quantified by calculating positives covered minus negatives covered minus the number of literals; for instance, a simpler rule covering 20 positives and 10 negatives may score higher than a more complex rule covering 21 positives and 9 negatives.

slides.title: - A loss function quantifies the impact or consequence of an error (incorrect prediction)
slides.summary: A loss function quantifies the impact or consequence of an incorrect prediction, such as 0/1-loss which assigns 0 for correct and 1 for incorrect predictions; its average represents the classification error rate. The primary goal is to find a hypothesis $h$ within the hypothesis space $\mathcal{H}$ that minimizes this loss on the data while simultaneously minimizing model size or complexity. This optimization balances reducing prediction error with controlling the weight of the model's size.

slides.title: - Lazy learners: there is no explicit model
slides.summary: Lazy learners do not construct an explicit model during training; instead, they build a new model on demand for each specific query by comparing the surroundings of the input to neighboring examples. This approach pushes all computational work to prediction time rather than learning phase. Practical applications include recommender systems that suggest similar items based on current queries and medical case comparisons, such as analyzing breast cancer cases against historical data.

slides.title: - Lazy learners: there is no explicit model
slides.summary: Lazy learners do not create an explicit model during training; instead, they build a new model on demand for each query, pushing all computational work to prediction time. In contrast, eager learners construct a single global model that applies to all examples, completing the necessary work at training time. This distinction highlights the fundamental difference in when and how these two approaches perform their modeling tasks.

slides.summary: This slide introduces a first classification attempt based on memorizing the training dataset $T = \{(x_i, y_i)\}$. To classify a new example $e$, the method checks if an identical instance exists in $T$ by comparing all $d$ attributes; if a match is found, it returns the corresponding label $y_i$. If no exact match exists, the algorithm returns an unknown result (?).

slides.title: Let T={(xi, yi)} where i ∈ {1,..,n}
slides.summary: This slide introduces a first classification attempt that memorizes the training set $T=\{(x_i, y_i)\}$ by returning the label $y_i$ only if an exact match is found for all features of example $e$. If no such instance exists in $T$, the method returns an unknown result (?). This approach is fundamentally limited because it cannot generalize beyond the specific training data and relies on a very restrictive exact-match condition.

slides.title: - Find the k nearest labelled examples and return their combined decision
slides.summary: To classify an example $e$ using k-Nearest Neighbors, the algorithm identifies the $k$ nearest labeled examples from the training set $T$. It maintains a priority queue of size $k$, updating it by adding any example $(x_j, y_j)$ whose distance to $e$ is less than the current maximum distance in the queue. The final prediction is generated by combining the labels ($y_j$) of the $k$ examples stored in the priority queue.

slides.title: - Find the k nearest labelled examples and return their combined decision
slides.summary: The k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) algorithm classifies a test example by identifying the $k$ closest training instances using a distance measure and combining their labels to form a prediction. While simple majority voting is common, the professor notes that distance can serve as a weighting parameter where closer neighbors exert more influence. A critical concern highlighted for exams is handling features with different scales; without normalization techniques like min-max normalization, distance calculations become skewed by larger numerical ranges.

slides.title: What distances are possible?
slides.summary: What distances are possible?

slides.title: - Similarities: Higher number = more similar → neighbors are most similar
slides.summary: Similarities and distances operate inversely: higher similarity values indicate greater resemblance, while higher distance values indicate objects are farther apart, making neighbors the closest points. Distances must satisfy four constraints: non-negativity, zero self-distance, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. While distances can be converted to similarities using the formula $sim(i,j) = 1 / (1 + Dist(i,j))$, the reverse conversion is not possible because these mathematical constraints apply only to distances, not similarities.

slides.title: - All discrete features: Hamming distance counts the number of features
slides.summary: For all discrete features, Hamming distance counts the number of features on which two examples differ by assigning zero if values match and one if they do not. A higher Hamming distance indicates more differing feature values between the instances. The slide also lists Manhattan and Euclidean distances as classic measures for real-valued features, while the professor notes that advanced metrics like value difference exist specifically for probabilities.

slides.title: - Value difference metric: attribute values are close if they make similar
slides.summary: The value difference metric treats attribute values as close when they lead to similar predictions, which helps compare mixed continuous and discrete attributes.

slides.title: - Jaccard similarity:
slides.summary: Jaccard similarity measures set comparison by calculating the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union. Jaccard distance is defined as one minus the Jaccard similarity, representing how distant two sets are. These formulas appear on the exam formula sheet; for example, if the intersection of sets S1 and S2 has a size of 3, the resulting similarity is 0.3 and the distance is 0.7.

slides.title: - Edit distance for strings: the number of required edits to transform a string into another
slides.summary: Edit distance for strings is defined as the number of required edits to transform one string into another. For instance, transforming "learning" to "leaning" requires one edit (removing 'r'), while changing "learning" to "carving" requires three edits: removing 'l', replacing 'e' with 'c', and replacing 'n' with 'v'. This concept applies to structured objects like text, distinct from numerical vector similarities such as cosine similarity.

slides.title: How can we combine
slides.summary: For classification, neighbors’ labels can be combined by majority vote; for regression, their target values can be averaged.

slides.title: - Majority vote
slides.summary: While standard k-NN uses majority voting, this approach is insufficient for cases like 5-NN where neighbor distances vary. The solution is distance-weighted k-NN, which predicts the class by maximizing the sum of weights for each label, where the weight $w_i$ is inversely proportional to the squared distance between the query point and the neighbor.

slides.title: - Average of the nearest neighbors
slides.summary: The lecture introduces the method of using the average of the nearest neighbors to predict real values within the k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) framework. This approach distinguishes regression tasks, which output continuous numerical results, from classification tasks that typically assign discrete categories. The core mechanism involves calculating the mean of the target values from the identified nearest neighbors to generate the final prediction.

slides.title: - Average of the nearest neighbors
slides.summary: While k-NN is commonly used for classification, it can also predict real numerical values through regression by calculating the average of the nearest neighbors' values. This approach addresses limitations in standard classification where distance weighting might be necessary to account for varying proximity among neighbors. Instead of assigning a single class label, the algorithm computes the mean of the target values from the selected k-nearest neighbors to generate a continuous prediction.

slides.title: - Average of the nearest neighbors
slides.summary: To predict real values using k-nearest neighbors (kNN), a local regression model serves as an alternative solution to simply averaging the nearest neighbors. This approach involves learning a specific model on the $k$ nearest neighbors and then utilizing that local model to generate the final prediction.

slides.title: • Voronoi diagram: neighboring cells may make the same prediction
slides.summary: A Voronoi diagram partitions the feature space into regions where every point is closer to a specific node than any other, defined by bisector lines between pairs of nodes. While neighboring cells in this diagram may make the same prediction, the decision surface specifically separates regions that yield different predictions. By applying this construction to all training example pairs, the entire space can be partitioned based on proximity to these nodes.

slides.title: - Small k: each example can have a large effect on prediction → scattered
slides.summary: A small $k$ value creates rough, scattered decision surfaces where individual examples exert a large influence, increasing the risk of overfitting. Conversely, a large $k$ introduces an averaging effect that limits each example's impact, resulting in smoother surfaces but raising the risk of underfitting. Selecting the optimal $k$ requires balancing these opposing risks to avoid losing meaningful patterns while preventing excessive sensitivity to noise.

slides.title: - Iterate over different ‘k’ values, different distance measures, …
slides.summary: To select optimal k-NN parameters, iterate over different 'k' values and distance measures using the training set as neighbors. Evaluate performance on the validation set to identify the best configuration by tweaking these parameters repeatedly. Once optimized, use the test set solely to evaluate the final model against other approaches, ensuring the training, validation, and test sets serve their distinct roles in parameter selection and comparison.

slides.title: - Min-max normalization: Map between 0 and 1 →
slides.summary: Min-max normalization maps data values to a range between 0 and 1. The slide illustrates this by transforming raw BPM and Energy measurements, such as 50 and 1.5, into normalized values like 0 and 0.96. This process scales the original dataset so that the minimum value becomes 0 and the maximum value becomes 1, with intermediate values proportionally adjusted.

slides.title: - Min-max normalization: Map between 0 and 1 →
slides.summary: Min-max normalization maps attribute values to a range between 0 and 1 by subtracting the variable's minimum and dividing by the difference between its maximum and minimum. For example, with BPM values ranging from 50 to 175, a value of 170 normalizes to 0.96. This technique is preferred when distance matters, whereas standardization alternatively uses the mean and standard deviation to scale data.

slides.title: - Irrelevant features dominate distance
slides.summary: Irrelevant features can dominate distance measures, leading to poor classification performance. To address this, solutions include leveraging domain knowledge to carefully select the feature space, applying weights to prioritize relevant attributes over less important ones like duration, or reducing dimensionality to automatically retain only significant features.

slides.title: - Weird things happen in high dimensions because our intuitions from low-
slides.summary: The curse of dimensionality arises because intuitions from low-dimensional spaces do not translate to high-dimensional ones, creating significant problems for learners. Adding many features can lead to spurious correlations and mislead kNN algorithms as data density lowers, causing distances to flatten until all examples appear equidistant. This phenomenon occurs when moving from 2D to higher dimensions like 10 or 100, though it does not apply if the distribution of positives has low variance.

slides.title: - kNN is very slow
slides.summary: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) is computationally slow because every query requires computing distances across all training examples, resulting in O(nd) complexity where n is the number of examples and d is the dimension. This approach also necessitates storing all training data in memory. To improve efficiency, solutions include using efficient retrieval structures like KD trees, applying locality sensitive hashing to identify neighbors via hashes, or employing product quantization to compress data and approximate distances.

slides.title: - Advantages
slides.summary: k-NN offers fast training as a lazy model that defers computation to validation while easily learning complex target functions through varying k values. Its flexibility allows prediction of discrete, real, or probabilistic outputs across diverse data types by simply adjusting the distance measure, unlike specialized neural networks. Additionally, k-NN supports online incremental learning and shares reasoning elements with human cognition.

slides.title: Data: (X,Y) examples
slides.summary: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) is a lazy, instance-based supervised learning model that relaxes exact feature matching by assuming nearby examples share similar outputs. Prediction involves selecting $k$ nearest training instances based on a chosen distance measure and combining their labels, requiring careful choices regarding feature scaling and weighting. While intuitive, kNN faces pitfalls including high computational cost at test time, large memory requirements, and sensitivity to irrelevant features or dimensionality.
